analysis.one_liner: Blocks OSHA from issuing a rule requiring employers to protect workers from extreme heat.
analysis.headline: The House Education and Workforce Committee advanced the bill 18-15 on July 21, 2026; it has not yet received a House floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: OSHA proposed a rule in 2024 that would require employers to set up heat injury and illness prevention plans when the heat index reaches 80°F, with extra steps at 90°F, covering nearly every industry with heat-exposed workers. This bill would forbid the Labor Department from finalizing, putting in place, or enforcing that rule, or anything like it. It cleared a House committee by a narrow 18-15 vote and now waits for a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers in heat-exposed industries — construction, agriculture, warehousing, delivery, maritime work — would avoid the cost of writing and running heat prevention plans, providing water, shade, and rest breaks, and the risk of OSHA citations for heat hazards.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers in construction, agriculture, and warehousing

how_it_helps.text: The bill flatly prohibits the Secretary of Labor from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing OSHA's proposed 'Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings' rule, or any substantially similar standard.

The blocked rule would have required employers across general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture to create heat prevention plans triggered at heat indexes of 80°F and 90°F, so stopping it removes those compliance obligations entirely.

Without the rule, employers remain subject only to OSHA's general requirement to keep workplaces free of recognized hazards, an enforcement path that is less specific and less predictable than a written standard.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in hot outdoor and indoor jobs would continue to face heat illness and death without a specific federal standard requiring their employers to plan for it; OSHA would only be able to cite employers case-by-case under general hazard rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently block a rule that would have required heat prevention plans at an 80°F heat-index trigger, with additional protections at 90°F, for nearly all workers OSHA covers.

If the bill passes, OSHA would have no specific heat standard at all, leaving enforcement to the general duty clause — citations after a hazard is already recognized rather than plans that prevent it.

An honest supporter's strongest point: the proposed rule covers virtually every sector where OSHA has jurisdiction and would impose mandated plans on employers of every size, a cost that falls hardest on small businesses with lean safety staffs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is purely cost avoidance for employers; its cost is that the workers most exposed to heat — a hazard that kills — get no specific federal protection. OSHA's general-duty enforcement can penalize heat hazards after the fact but does not require the water, shade, rest, and planning steps a written standard would. Anyone weighing this honestly should note that the bill eliminates a protection rather than redesigning it, though the 80°F universal trigger and broad coverage are the fair targets of the cost objection.

outcome.mechanism: The House Education and Workforce Committee approved the bill 18-15 and sent it toward the floor, where it has not yet been scheduled for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Messmer introduced the bill on November 20, 2025, with 68 Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
On July 21, 2026, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported, as amended, by a recorded vote of 18-15.

The bill targets OSHA's proposed rule published August 30, 2024, which would cover general industry, construction, maritime, and agriculture and require employer heat plans at 80°F and 90°F heat-index triggers.
OSHA currently has no specific heat exposure standard and has relied on general authority and a National Emphasis Program to cite employers for heat violations.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers in heat-exposed industries: OSHA's proposed heat rule remains unfinalized, and this bill, if it became law, would lock that in permanently.

sides.party_line_note: All 68 cosponsors are Republicans, and the bill advanced through a Republican-run committee on a narrow 18-15 vote; the record does not break that vote down by party.

industries.note: The bill would spare them the proposed requirement to maintain heat prevention plans for crews working above the 80°F trigger; the cost of that protection is borne by their workers in heat-illness risk.
Farm work is among the most heat-exposed sectors the proposed rule covers; blocking it removes a mandate to provide planned water, shade, and rest protections.

industries.industry: Warehousing, delivery, and other hot-indoor employers
industries.note: The rule reached general industry and indoor work settings, not just fields and job sites; blocking it leaves indoor heat to case-by-case enforcement.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee but not the floor. Many bills reported out of committee never get a floor vote, though with 68 Republican cosponsors and a House majority of 223, a floor vote is plausible; passage in the Senate would be a much higher bar, and the bill could also die at year's end if never scheduled.
